title: The Devops Engineer Who Never Sleeps — Diamond Bishop, Datadog

primary.label: Agent Architecture & Harnesses
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 67%).

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk's primary focus is structuring AI agents for DevOps workflows, including hypothesis-driven investigation loops, planning, and multi-step agent harnesses. Agents target enterprise operations like on-call incident response and are built on Datadog's developer platform for software builders. The agents are in private beta, Datadog has shipped production AI features since 2015, and the talk outlines a future vision for DevSecOps agents for hire. Assumes familiarity with observability, on-call workflows, and agent architectures, targeting AI engineering practitioners. Recorded conference presentation at AI Engineer Summit 2025 in New York. All evidence anchors are graded as said_in_transcript with direct excerpts from the talk.

summary: Diamond Bishop introduces Datadog's AI agents initiative, called Bits AI, positioning it within Datadog's broader observability and security platform. Datadog has shipped AI features since around 2015 (proactive alerting, root cause analysis, impact analysis, change tracking), but Bishop sees a clear era shift driven by bigger, smarter, multimodal, reasoning-capable models and foundation model competition, comparable to the microprocessor or SaaS transitions, where intelligence becomes too cheap to meter. Datadog is moving up the stack to offer AI agents that use the platform on customers' behalf. Two private-beta agents are highlighted: the AI On-Call Engineer, which triggers on alerts, reads runbooks, investigates logs/metrics/traces in a hypothesis-driven loop, suggests remediations, and can write postmortems; and the AI Software Engineer (error tracking assistant), which analyzes errors, identifies causes, proposes code fixes, generates tests, and can create PRs or open diffs in VS Code. Bishop then shares lessons learned: scope tasks as jobs-to-be-done with measurable, verifiable steps, favoring vertical task-specific agents; design eval first—offline, online, and living evals with end-to-end measurements; build teams with one or two ML experts plus optimistic generalist engineers who are AI-augmented; UX matters more than expected and old patterns are changing, with Bishop favoring agents that work like human teammates; and observability remains essential. In the final section, Bishop introduces Datadog's LLM observability view, which groups hosted, self-run, and API-based model interactions into a single pane of glass. He shows an agent graph view that renders complex multi-step agent workflows (potentially hundreds of calls) as a human-readable graph with highlighted error nodes. He articulates an application-layer bitter lesson: general methods leveraging off-the-shelf models ultimately outperform fine-tuning, so teams should stay model-agnostic. He predicts agents will surpass humans as SaaS users within approximately five years and demonstrates a quick MCP integration letting Claude use Datadog directly. The vision is DevSecOps agents for hire per customer, handling on-call and operations, while other companies' coding and SRE agents become Datadog customers. Small companies can use tools like Cursor or Devon to build products, then use Datadog's agents for operations, enabling an order of magnitude more ideas to reach the real world.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.
temporalContext: Transcript claims reflect the publication date; linked external context was checked at the run's research date.
takeaways: Datadog sees an era shift with reasoning, multimodal models making intelligence too cheap to meter; two private-beta agents (AI On-Call Engineer and AI Software Engineer) are in development.
Scope agent tasks as jobs-to-be-done with measurable, verifiable steps; prefer vertical task-specific agents over generalized ones.
Eval must be designed first—offline, online, and living evals with end-to-end measurements; not thinking about eval first was a major recurring mistake.
Build teams with one or two ML experts plus optimistic AI-augmented generalist engineers who are excited to move fast in ambiguity.
UX matters more than backend engineers expect; Bishop favors agents that behave like human teammates rather than new pages or buttons.
LLM observability is essential for debugging complex agent workflows; Datadog's agent graph view renders hundreds of multi-step calls as a human-readable graph with highlighted error nodes.
An application-layer bitter lesson applies: general methods leveraging off-the-shelf models outperform fine-tuning, so teams should stay model-agnostic and easily swappable.
Agents will likely surpass humans as SaaS users within ~5 years; products should be built for agent customers via protocols like MCP, not just human users.
The vision is DevSecOps agents for hire per customer handling operations, while other companies' agents become Datadog customers.
Understand how Datadog structures AI agents for DevOps workflows, including on-call and software engineering agents.

sections.title: Introduction and Background
sections.summary: Diamond Bishop introduces himself, his 15-year AI career spanning Cortana, Alexa, PyTorch, and an AI DevOps startup (Augmend) acquired by Datadog, and his current role directing AI Engineering at Datadog building Bits AI.

sections.title: Datadog and the Era Shift in AI
sections.summary: Datadog is described as an observability and security platform. AI has been shipping since ~2015 in features like proactive alerting and root cause analysis. Bishop sees a clear era shift comparable to microprocessors or SaaS, with intelligence becoming too cheap to meter, and Datadog moving up the stack to provide AI agents that use the platform for customers.

sections.title: AI On-Call Engineer Agent
sections.summary: The on-call agent triggers on alerts, reads runbooks, investigates logs/metrics/traces in a hypothesis-driven loop, validates or invalidates hypotheses, suggests remediations, can tie into existing Datadog workflows, and writes postmortems. A new collaboration page lets users see hypotheses, steps taken, and ask follow-up questions to build trust.

sections.title: AI Software Engineer Agent
sections.summary: The AI software engineer proactively analyzes errors, identifies causes, proposes code fixes, generates tests (e.g., recursion test), and can create a GitHub PR or open a diff in VS Code, reducing manual engineering time and on-call incidents.

sections.title: Lessons Learned: Scoping, Eval, Team, UX, Observability
sections.summary: Bishop shares lessons: scope tasks as jobs-to-be-done with measurable steps, favoring vertical agents; design eval first (offline, online, living); use domain experts as design partners not rule-writers; build teams with one or two ML experts plus optimistic AI-augmented generalists; UX matters more than expected and old patterns are changing; observability remains essential. The section ends segueing into observability for agents.

sections.title: LLM Observability, the Agent Bitter Lesson, and the Future
sections.summary: Bishop introduces Datadog's LLM observability view, grouping hosted, self-run, and API-based model interactions into a single pane of glass. He shows an agent graph view that renders complex multi-step agent workflows as a human-readable graph with highlighted error nodes. He articulates an application-layer bitter lesson: general methods leveraging off-the-shelf models outperform fine-tuning, so teams should stay model-agnostic. He predicts agents will surpass humans as SaaS users within ~5 years and shows a quick MCP integration letting Claude use Datadog directly. The vision is DevSecOps agents for hire per customer handling operations, while other companies' agents become Datadog customers. Small companies can use tools like Cursor or Devon to build products, then use Datadog's agents for operations, enabling an order of magnitude more ideas to reach the real world.

demonstrations: AI Software Engineer catching a recursion issue, proposing a fix, and creating a recursion test, with option to create a GitHub PR or open diff in VS Code.
AI On-Call Engineer running proactive investigations, pulling summaries before the human reaches their computer, showing hypotheses and steps taken from runbooks.
New page for human-AI collaboration letting users see why a hypothesis was generated, what the agent found, and ask follow-up questions.
Datadog's agent graph view showing complex multi-step agent workflows as a human-readable graph with bright red nodes highlighting errors.
MCP integration setting up Claude to use Datadog directly, configured relatively quickly.
limitations: Building demos quickly is easy but verifying and improving agent behavior over time is very hard.
There aren't many ML experts available to go around, so teams cannot rely on staffing entirely with ML specialists.
Generalized agents are less effective than vertical task-specific ones for measurable, verifiable work.
Agent observability can get messy fast with hundreds of calls and complex multi-step workflows that are impossible to debug from a flat list.
Fine-tuning specific models can be quickly overtaken when new off-the-shelf models are released, making heavy investment in model-specific work risky.
quantitativeClaims: Datadog has been shipping AI features since around 2015.
Diamond Bishop has about 15 years of AI/ML career experience.
Agents may surpass humans as users of SaaS products within approximately 5 years.
Datadog's agent workflows can involve hundreds of calls across complex multi-step processes.
